question: The Commission is considering limiting the role national antitrust bodies play in enforcing competition rules by centralising decisions in Brussels. This idea is a step in the wrong direction. Member States have the best understanding of their own markets and have instruments that are adapted to local realities.

Poland, like France and Germany, has put rules in place to protect small- and medium-sized enterprises from abuse from larger contractors – even where the EU would not formally identify the contractor as ‘dominant’.

National institutions such as Poland’s Office of Competition and Consumer Protection (UOKiK) are able to respond swiftly to local problems, while the Commission almost exclusively focuses on a few global giants. Taking this responsibility away from Member States would weaken the protection of SMEs, which form the backbone of the EU’s economy.
A balance between EU and national competences is needed, rather than centralisation and bureaucratisation. In light of the above: 1.
Why does the Commission want to prevent Member States from applying their own, stricter rules protecting SMEs?
How does the Commission justify centralisation, given that, in practice, it only focuses on the biggest technological companies and global mergers?
Does the Commission recognise that eliminating national competences would impact local businesses and consumers, undermining the effectiveness of protecting competition on the single market?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.2.2026) The Commission does not wish to prevent Member States from protecting small and mediumsized enterprises (SMEs). To the contrary, the Commission considers that a framework for the coherent and effective enforcement of competition rules in the EU is the best way to promote competitive markets, to the benefit of businesses (including SMEs) and consumers alike.

In the context of the review of Regulation 1/2003 and based on the results of an evaluation exercise1, the Commission is considering, how to address the risk of fragmented competition law enforcement that has been associated to the (increased) use of stricter national laws on unilateral conduct.

In this context, the Commission is assessing whether it would be appropriate to further harmonise unilateral conduct rules at EU level, or instead to expand the existing coordination and information exchange mechanisms within the European Competition Network, to ensure coherence, complementarity, and effectiveness of EU and national laws.

The Commission is currently carrying an impact assessment of the available options, which is expected to be concluded in the third quarter of 2026. The Commission is not centralising decisions enforcing EU competition law.

Under Regulation 1/2003, both the Commission and national competition authorities are competent to apply EU competition rules (Articles 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union) and must do so in close cooperation. As the evaluation has shown, this system of decentralised enforcement is a major success of Regulation 1/2003.
EU competition law plays a key role in promoting competitive markets, and the Commission does not envisage eliminating national competences relating to its enforcement.
